title: Lean Community Certifies Claude-Aided Riemann Hypothesis
summary: Lean and Mathlib communities officially verified Levent Alpöge's 17-million-line Claude-aided proof of the Riemann Hypothesis on November 22, 2026.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Lean and Mathlib communities officially certified Levent Alpöge's Claude-aided proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as correct on November 22, 2026.
- MIT verification confirmed all 175,187 modules compiled with zero errors under Lean 4.33.1, satisfying every formal correctness criterion.
- The 17-million-line proof marks the first time a major mathematical conjecture has been solved with AI assistance and formal verification.


On November 22, 2026, the Lean and Mathlib communities issued a joint statement certifying Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as correct. The verification followed a 24-hour intensive review of the 17-million-line Lean codebase, which Alpöge released two days earlier with assistance from Anthropic's Claude model. The certification marks the first time a major unsolved mathematical conjecture has been proven using AI-assisted methods and formal verification.


## Verification Process and Technical Validation


Andrew Sutherland at MIT led the technical verification effort, confirming that all 175,187 modules in Alpöge's proof compiled successfully under Lean 4.33.1 and Mathlib dependencies. The compilation process ran for approximately 24 hours with zero errors, satisfying the first criterion outlined in the Lean community's verification standards published November 12, 2026. Two independent tools, comparator and con-leche, performed statement-matching checks to confirm the library's theorem exactly matched Mathlib's formalization of the Riemann Hypothesis.


The proof kernel checks verified every logical step in the 17-million-line codebase followed valid inference rules. The Lean proof assistant's type-checking system ensured no gaps existed in the mathematical reasoning, a level of rigor impossible to achieve through traditional peer review alone.


## Community Response and Endorsement


The Lean Formalization Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative both endorsed the joint certification statement. The communities praised Alpöge's achievement and noted the collaborative effort required to verify such a massive proof in under 48 hours. Dozens of Lean developers contributed computational resources and expertise to accelerate the verification timeline, demonstrating the strength of open mathematical communities in validating formal proofs.


The statement specifically acknowledged that the codebase depends solely on Mathlib, ensuring all dependencies are publicly auditable and previously verified. This architectural decision simplified the verification process and increased confidence in the result.


## Release Date and Proof Architecture


Officially released on November 20, 2026, Alpöge's proof represents a collaboration between human mathematical insight and AI-assisted formalization. While Alpöge directed the proof strategy and high-level architecture, Claude helped translate mathematical ideas into Lean's formal language and suggested intermediate lemmas. The 17-million-line scale reflects the extreme detail required for machine-verifiable proofs compared to traditional mathematical papers.


The codebase structure follows Mathlib conventions, organizing the proof into modules covering analytic number theory, complex analysis, and specialized results about the zeta function. This modular architecture allowed parallel verification by multiple community members.


## Implications for Mathematical Research


The certification establishes a new standard for mathematical proof verification in the AI era. Traditional peer review of a proof this complex could take years and still miss subtle errors. Formal verification in Lean provides absolute certainty, with every logical step checked by a proof kernel immune to human oversight failures.


The success also validates AI-assisted formalization as a viable approach for attacking historically intractable problems. Alpöge's method combining Claude's language understanding with Lean's formal rigor may accelerate progress on other unsolved conjectures, though the Riemann Hypothesis remains unique in its centrality to number theory.


## What This Means


The Lean community's certification of Alpöge's proof demonstrates that AI-assisted mathematics has reached a milestone where machine-verified proofs can resolve century-old conjectures. While the mathematical community will spend years understanding the new ideas in Alpöge's approach, the formal verification guarantees correctness beyond any doubt. This achievement sets a precedent for future collaborations between AI systems, proof assistants, and human mathematicians tackling the hardest problems in mathematics.
